The '''Landau kernel''' is named after the German [[Number theory|number theorist]] [[Edmund Landau]]. The kernel is a [[summability kernel]] defined as:<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Terras |first=Audrey |date=May 25, 2009 |title=Lecture 8. Dirac and Weierstrass |url=https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~aterras/ma142blecture8.pdf}}</ref>

<math display="block">L_n (t) = \begin{cases}
        \frac{(1-t^2)^n}{c_n} & \text{if } {-1} \leq t \leq 1\\
        0 & \text{otherwise} 
    \end{cases}</math>where the coefficients <math>c_n</math> are defined as follows:

<math display="block">c_n = \int_{-1}^1 (1-t^2)^n \, dt. </math>

== Visualisation ==
Using integration by parts, one can show that:<ref>{{cite book
 | last = Hilber | first = Courant
 | title = Methods of Mathematical Physics, Vol. I
 | pages = 84
}}</ref>
<math display="block">c_n = \frac{(n!)^2 \, 2^{2n+1}}{(2n)! (2n+1)}. </math>
Hence, this implies that the Landau kernel can be defined as follows: <math display="block">L_n (t) = \begin{cases}
(1-t^2)^n \frac{(2n)! (2n+1)}{(n!)^2 \, 2^{2n+1}} & \text{for } t \in [-1,1]\\
0 & \text{elsewhere}
\end{cases}
</math>

Plotting this function for different values of ''n'' reveals that as ''n'' goes to infinity, <math> L_n(t) </math> approaches the [[Dirac delta function]] as a [[Distribution (mathematical analysis)|distribution]], as seen in the image,<ref name=":0" /> where the following functions are plotted.

== Properties ==
Some general properties of the Landau kernel is that it is nonnegative and continuous on <math>\mathbb{R}</math>. These properties are made more concrete in the following section.

=== Dirac sequences ===
{{Math theorem
| math_statement = A Dirac sequence is a sequence <math> \{ K_n(t) \} </math> of functions <math> K_n(t) \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}</math> that satisfies the following properities:
* <math> K_n(t) \geq 0, \, \, \forall t \in \mathbb{R} \text{ and } \forall n \in \mathbb{Z} </math> 
* <math> \int_{-\infty}^\infty K_n (t) \, dt =1, \, \forall n </math>
* <math> \forall \varepsilon >0 \, \forall \delta >0 \, \exists N \in \mathbb{Z}_+ \, \forall n \geq N :</math> <br> <math> {} \quad \int_{\mathbb{R} \smallsetminus [-\delta,\delta]}K_n(t) \, dt= \int_{-\infty}^{-\delta} K_n (t) \, dt + \int_\delta^\infty K_n (t) \, dt < \varepsilon </math>
| name = Definition: Dirac sequence
}}
The third bullet point means that the area under the graph of the function <math>y = K_n(t)</math> becomes increasingly concentrated close to the origin as ''n'' approaches infinity. This definition lends us to the following theorem.
{{Math theorem
| math_statement = The sequence of Landau kernels is a Dirac sequence
}}
<u>Proof</u>: We prove the third property only. In order to do so, we introduce the following lemma:
{{Math theorem
| math_statement = The coefficients satsify the following relationship, <math> c_n \geq \frac{2}{n+1}</math>
| name = Lemma
}}
<u>Proof of the Lemma:</u>

Using the definition of the coefficients above, we find that the integrand is even, we may write<math display="block">\frac{c_n}{2} = \int_{0}^1 (1-t^2)^n \, dt = \int_0^1 (1-t)^n(1+t)^n \, dt \geq \int_0^1 (1-t)^n \, dt = \frac{1}{1+n}</math>completing the proof of the lemma. A corollary of this lemma is the following:
{{Math theorem
| math_statement = For all positive, real <math> \delta :  </math> <math> \int_{\mathbb{R} \smallsetminus [-\delta,\delta]}K_n(t) \, dt \leq \frac{2}{c_n} \int_\delta^1 (1-t^2)^n \, dt \leq (n+1)(1-\delta^2)^n </math>
| name = Corollary
}}
